fable-5.1.text:
The way I look at it, there are two things going on at the same time, and you have to see them together or you'll misunderstand both.

The first is the trend. Over any long stretch of time, the single most important thing is productivity, and productivity comes from people learning, inventing, and applying what they learn. That's why, if you look at a chart of real income per person over the last few hundred years, it goes up and to the right. That upward slope is almost entirely human inventiveness and technology. Wars, depressions, pandemics, they're little wiggles on that chart. So when people ask me what I'm most optimistic about, it's that.

The second thing is the cycles that go around that trend line. The most important one is the debt cycle. There's a short one, roughly every five to eight years, that most people recognize as the business cycle, and there's a long one, which runs maybe 75 or 100 years, where debt builds up relative to income until it can't be serviced and the system has to restructure. Those cycles happen because of human nature, not because of technology. People borrow against the future when times are good, they overextend, and then there's a reckoning.

Now, here's where the two interact. Every big new technology creates a boom, and the boom almost always turns into a bubble, because people correctly see that the technology is transformative and then incorrectly assume the prices can only go one way. Canals, railroads, radio and electricity in the 1920s, the internet in 1999. The technology was real in every one of those cases, and in every one of those cases most of the money that chased it was lost, because the excitement got financed with debt and the debt cycle did what debt cycles do. I think it's likely we're in a version of that with AI right now. The technology is going to change everything, and that does not mean the investments in it are going to pay off at today's prices.

The other interaction, which I think people underestimate, is that technology raises productivity but it doesn't distribute the gains evenly. It makes some people very rich and makes other people's skills obsolete, and that widens the wealth gap. Historically, large wealth gaps combined with a debt bust are what produce internal conflict, populism, the left and the right fighting, and that's one of the other big forces I study. So technology is the thing that lifts us all over time, and it's also one of the things that puts stress on the system in the short run.

So my answer is, don't choose between them. Technology is the trend, cycles are the oscillation around the trend, and the mistake is to look at one and forget the other.

opus-5.5.text:
Well, the way I look at it, there are really two things going on at the same time, and you have to separate them to understand what's happening.

The first is a long, upward-sloping line, and that's productivity. Over time, people learn, they invent, they get better at doing things, and that raises living standards. That's mostly what technology is. If you look back over hundreds of years, that line just keeps going up. It's the most important force over the long run.

The second is the cycles that swing around that line, and those are mostly about debt and money. A short-term debt cycle lasts maybe six to ten years, and that's what most people call the business cycle. Then there's the big long-term debt cycle, roughly 75 years or so, where debts keep building up relative to incomes until they can't be serviced anymore, and then there's a big restructuring, money gets printed, and the order changes. Those cycles aren't driven by technology. They're driven by human nature and by how credit works. Credit lets you spend more than you earn today, but it means you have to spend less than you earn later. That basic dynamic plays out over and over again.

Now, the interesting thing is how the two interact. When there's a big technological breakthrough, it almost always gets financed with a lot of credit and a lot of speculation, because people correctly see that it's going to change the world but they extrapolate and they overpay. You saw it with the railroads, with radio and autos in the 1920s, with the internet in the late '90s. The technology was real. The productivity gains were real. But the financial bubble around it was also real, and when that bubble burst it caused a lot of pain, even though the technology went on to transform everything. So you can be right about the technology and still lose a lot of money.

The other big thing is that new technologies tend to widen the gaps: the gaps in wealth, in opportunity, in values. The people and companies at the cutting edge do extraordinarily well, and a lot of others get left behind. When you combine that with a lot of debt and an economic downturn, you get internal conflict, populism of the left and the right, and that's what we're seeing now. And technology is also what determines who's most powerful in the world, economically and militarily, which is why you have this great power conflict between the United States and China, a lot of which is a technology war.

So, with artificial intelligence, I think we're at one of those moments. It's going to produce enormous productivity gains, probably more than anything we've seen. But it's arriving at a time when we're late in the long-term debt cycle, with big deficits, big internal divisions, and big geopolitical conflict. The question isn't whether the technology is good. It is. The question is whether we handle all these other forces well enough to get the benefits without tearing ourselves apart in the process. History tells us those are the things you have to watch together, not separately. Most people look at them one at a time, and that's how they get surprised.

fable-5.text:
Well, the way I look at it is that there are really two forces operating at the same time, and you have to see them both to understand what's going on.

The first is the evolution of man's inventiveness — learning, technology, productivity. That's the upward trend line. Over any period of time, people learn, they invent, and that raises living standards. If you look at a chart of output per person over the last five hundred years, it just keeps rising, and technology is the main driver of that. The printing press, the Industrial Revolution, computers, and now AI — these things change what a person can produce, and that's what really raises wealth over the long run.

But around that upward trend line, you have cycles. And the most important one is the debt cycle, because the way economies work, credit creates buying power — it lets you spend more than you earn — and that's stimulative on the way up, but it creates an obligation to pay back, which is depressing on the way down. So you get these swings. There's the short-term debt cycle, the business cycle, which runs maybe eight years, and then the long-term debt cycle, which runs fifty, seventy-five years, where debts build up relative to incomes until you can't keep doing it, and then you get a big restructuring — like 1929 to '33, or 2008.

Now, here's where the two interact, and this is the important part. Technology raises productivity, but it doesn't raise it evenly. It creates big winners and it displaces people, so it widens the wealth gap. And when you have a large wealth gap at the same time that you have a downturn in the debt cycle — when the economic pie is shrinking and people are fighting over how to divide it — that's when you get internal conflict, populism of the left and populism of the right. We saw that in the 1930s and we're seeing a version of it now.

So technology is the reason we're richer than our grandparents, and it will be the reason our grandchildren are richer than us. But it doesn't eliminate the cycles — people always extrapolate the good times, they borrow too much, and the cycle turns. And studying history, what I've found is that most of the big surprises in my life were things that never happened in my lifetime but happened many times before. The machine works the same way over and over again. If you understand the cause-effect relationships — how productivity, debt, and the gaps between people interact — then what's happening today isn't surprising. It's just the cycle playing out again, this time with AI as the new technology running through it.

opus-5.text:
Well, the way I think about it — and I have to explain how I came to think about it, because I'm a mechanic, I'm not a theorist. I invest. I've been doing this for over fifty years, and what happened repeatedly in my career is that something would hit me that had never happened in my lifetime but had happened many times before in history. The 1971 devaluation of the dollar, the 2008 debt crisis, the pandemic. So I was forced to study history, and when you study five hundred years of it, you see that there are really two different things going on at the same time, and people confuse them.

There's a trend line, and there are cycles around the trend line. The trend line is upward, and the thing that produces that upward trend line is inventiveness — learning, technology, productivity. That's the only reason your standard of living is many, many times better than your great-grandparents'. Not because of monetary policy, not because of politics. Because human beings learn things and the learning compounds, and the learning doesn't get destroyed in the same way wealth does. And then there are the cycles around that trend line, and those are mostly about credit and debt and politics and human nature, and those are the things that feel enormous when you're living through them and are oscillations when you look back.

Now here's where they interact, and this is the part that I think is most important. Big technological revolutions almost always come with big debt bubbles, because a new technology creates a plausible story about the future, and plausible stories about the future are what people lend against. The canals, the railroads, electrification and the twenties, the dot-coms. And so you get the pattern: the technology is real, the productivity gain is real, and the financial claims on that productivity gain get priced far beyond what the productivity can service. Then you get the bust, the debt gets restructured or monetized, a lot of people lose a lot of money — and the technology stays. The railroads didn't get taken up when the railroad companies went bankrupt.

The second interaction is more troubling. Technology raises the pie but it doesn't distribute it, and typically it distributes it toward capital and toward a small number of highly educated people in a few places. So you get a widening wealth and opportunity gap at the same time you get the productivity boom. And when you have large wealth gaps and large debts and then a downturn, that's when you get internal conflict, populism, people on both extremes, fighting over how to divide the pie rather than how to grow it. That combination — high debt, big wealth gaps, a technology revolution, and a rising power challenging an existing power — that configuration has happened before and it never resolves quietly.

So when people ask me about AI, I say: I'm confident it raises the trend line. What I'm watching is whether we're wise enough to handle the cycle it's arriving inside of.

sonnet-5.5.text:
Let me describe how I see it as a mechanism. Over long stretches of time, humans have gotten better at things, so productivity rises. That's the upward trend line, and technology is the biggest driver of it. Around that line you get the cycles. They come mostly from credit and debt: when people borrow to buy things, it creates spending, and spending creates the income and the sense of prosperity that make them want to borrow more. That's the self-reinforcing part.

Technology and cycles collide in a particular way. When a transformative technology comes along, whether it's railroads, electricity, the automobile, the internet, or now AI, there's a real, legitimate reason to be excited, because the technology really will change the world. But then people project that into the future, extrapolate it, and bid up the prices of the companies they think are going to benefit. Credit follows, because people borrow to buy those assets. So you get a bubble, with a true story at the center of it. The technology is real and the bubble is real, and the two aren't contradictory.

Then the bubble bursts, because the cash flows can't support the debt that was used to buy the assets. Usually that happens when the central bank tightens, or when the debt-service burden gets too heavy. People who say "this time is different" overlook that being right about the technology doesn't make you right about the price you paid for it. Many railroad investors were right that railroads would change the world, and they still lost a lot of money. The technology survives and the particular financial structure doesn't.

So I think of technology as the thing that raises living standards over time, and the debt and credit cycle as the thing that determines the path you take there, the booms and the busts. That path matters a lot, because when a bust is bad, it creates political and social conflict. It affects who wins and who loses, and technology tends to widen that gap. Some people benefit enormously while others are displaced. That fuels the wealth and political divisions we're seeing now, and in history that's often when things get most volatile.

I try to keep both ideas in mind: the progress is real, and the cycle is real. If you're only focused on one of them, you'll get blindsided.

haiku-5.5.text:
Technology is one of the main engines of long-term prosperity, but I don't think it cancels the cycle. What it does is raise productivity, and productivity is what ultimately makes a country richer. The cycle runs on something more basic, which is credit. People borrow against their expected future income, and when spending is financed by debt, an economy can run hot for a long time before the debts become large relative to the income needed to service them.

Technology tends to accelerate both sides of that. When a major new technology arrives, whether it's electrification, the internet, or now AI, it creates real productivity gains. It also creates a story about how valuable the future is going to be. Investors and lenders get excited, they extend credit to finance the buildout, and asset prices rise faster than the cash flows underneath them. That's where bubbles come from. Some of the investment is genuinely valuable and some is wasted, and you usually only know which in hindsight.

Then comes the adjustment. Money gets tight, the weakest borrowers fail, and there's a period of pain. What happens next matters a great deal. Central banks and governments usually respond by easing and adding liquidity to cushion the decline, which keeps the cycle going in a new form. Over time, that pattern has left most major economies with more debt relative to their incomes than they had before.

So I see technology as a long-term driver of rising living standards, while the shorter cycles are driven largely by how debt and the psychology around it build up and unwind. The two interact. Technology creates the opportunities, and the credit cycle determines how much of that opportunity gets overbuilt and how painful the correction is.

My advice would be to welcome the progress, but don't confuse a great technology with a great investment, and watch the debt more closely than the headlines.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to distinguish between productivity and the cycle. Over time, we learn, we invent things, and we become capable of producing more with the same resources. Technology is a major driver of that. But that progress doesn’t happen in a straight line, and it doesn’t eliminate the effects of borrowing and lending.

When you borrow, you can spend more than you earn. That helps somebody else’s income, and the economy expands. But eventually you have to service that debt, which can mean spending less. So you have these movements around the longer-term path of productivity.

And the two interact. A new technology can create real opportunities, but it can also create tremendous excitement. People extrapolate, prices rise, and they borrow against those rising prices. You can have a technology that changes the world and still have investors lose money because they paid too much or used too much debt.

So I would ask two separate questions: What is this technology doing to our ability to produce? And what expectations and financial commitments have people built around it? Those can have very different answers.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to distinguish between the underlying progress and the cycles around that progress. Technology allows us to do more with less. We learn, we invent, we become more productive, and that raises our potential standard of living over time. But it doesn’t mean we move forward in a straight line.

The cycles have a lot to do with credit and human behavior. When people are optimistic, they borrow more, spend more, and bid up the prices of assets. That borrowing creates purchasing power today, but it also creates an obligation to pay later. Eventually, those obligations can grow faster than the income available to service them, and you get a reversal.

Technology can actually contribute to that excitement. People see a real breakthrough, correctly recognize that it will change things, and then assume almost any price is justified. So you can have a technology that succeeds and an investment in that technology that performs terribly. Those are two different judgments.

The important question is: are we increasing our capacity to produce, or are we increasing spending through debt? Both can look like prosperity for a while, but they have different consequences. Technological progress can continue through a downturn, even while debts are being restructured and asset prices are falling. Progress doesn’t eliminate the cycle, and the cycle doesn’t necessarily stop progress.

luna-5.6.text:
Technological progress is one of the great forces that raises productivity and living standards, but it doesn’t eliminate economic cycles—it changes their character. New technologies create periods of optimism, investment, and rapid growth, often accompanied by easy credit and rising asset prices. Then, as debts accumulate and expectations get ahead of reality, the cycle turns: weaker players fail, capital is reallocated, and the economy adjusts.

Over the long run, technology expands the size of the economic pie. But in the short run, who benefits—and who is displaced—depends on how quickly institutions, education, capital, and policy adapt. That’s why technological revolutions can produce both extraordinary prosperity and significant inequality and conflict during the transition.

luna-6.text: I think technological progress and economic cycles operate on different time scales. Technology can steadily raise productivity and create entirely new industries, but it doesn’t remove the forces that drive cycles—credit expanding and contracting, people responding to incentives and fear, and wealth being distributed unevenly. In fact, a major technology boom can bring both real gains and speculative excess. It can also displace workers before new opportunities reach them, widening gaps and creating political tension. So progress can make the economy more capable over the long run, while the familiar cycles of borrowing, investment, adjustment, and renewal continue along the way.
